summary:
Police action is the most serious documented risk to a trans visitor. In September 2017 officers in Baku detained at least 100 people in raids presented as action against prostitution; detainees were beaten, interrogated, subjected to forced medical examinations and blackmailed. A United States State Department report covering that period recorded threats of rape and the use of electric shocks. At least 60 of those held were imprisoned or fined, and the detentions formed part of a wave of arrests ahead of the Islamic Solidarity Games.

Accountability for those arrests has been pursued outside Azerbaijan. Human Rights Watch called in October 2017 for an investigation and for releases. Azerbaijan acknowledged the cases in 2019, and in April 2024 the European Court of Human Rights issued a ruling on the arrests and the mistreatment.

Raiding of private gatherings did not end with 2017. In July 2023 officers entered a private birthday party in Baku, where queer guests were subjected to forced medical examinations, physical and sexual harassment, and threats of outing.

Violence against trans people has been met with an inadequate official response. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 records the murder of a trans woman in Baku in March 2024 and an inadequate police investigation into it.

Legal protection is close to absent. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is not prohibited. Trans people cannot change the gender marker on official documents, though they may change their name to match their gender identity. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex has no route to recognition: marriage and civil unions in that category are neither recognised nor performed, and couples in it may not adopt children.

ILGA-Europe has ranked Azerbaijan last, 49th of 49, in Europe every year since 2015, citing a near total absence of legal protection.

Hostility is carried by state-affiliated and private media alike. QueeRadar monitoring found 77% of 428 media pieces analysed in 2023 to be hateful or biased against LGBTIQ people. In 2024 the state-affiliated Real TV aired discriminatory hate speech against LGBTI people after a Women's Day march demanding access to trans healthcare. In 2023 an activist was told to remove a rainbow flag from a Baku cafe.
tangentialFactors:
A 2017 United States State Department report recorded interference with expression, assembly and association through intimidation, incarceration on questionable charges and the blocking of websites, an environment in which the documented raids took place.

Media have been criticised for spreading fear and hate toward queer people through discriminatory language, and politicians and officials have used that language to shape public perception. A commentator on the Minority Azerbaijan webpage criticised this unprofessionalism.

LGBTQIA+ media nonetheless exists in the country. gay.az, the first news website for LGBTQIA+ people, launched on 25 May 2011, and Minority Magazine, the first LGBTQIA+ online magazine, was founded in December 2015 and became an NGO in August 2017. A documentary about a trans man premiered in Baku on 25 November 2017 with Dutch embassy support and drew about 80 people.

The age of consent is 16 for both heterosexual and homosexual sex. By law, no groups are excluded from blood donation apart from people infected with HIV/AIDS.

Critics have argued that Azerbaijan should not be allowed to host international events because of its discrimination against LGBTQIA+ people, a controversy that flared around the 2012 Eurovision contest held in the country.
localsOnly:
Discrimination has direct economic effects on trans residents. Trans people are rejected from jobs and housing and pushed into black-market work and precarious housing; one profiled 29-year-old trans woman was arrested, denied housing and employment, and left dependent on community support after her trans-friendly employer closed.

A shadow report to the 44th session of the United Nations committee overseeing CEDAW documents state-approved ignorance, employment discrimination, militant homophobia and transphobia in official and private media, forced marriages, and the impossibility of changing identity documents for trans women. The organisation that filed it serves more than 200 LBT people.

In 2024 a family forcibly transported an 18-year-old woman to Baku after she came out, according to the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025.

Azerbaijan mandates conscription for able-bodied men aged 18 to 35. Under the Regulation on Military Medical Examinations, LGBTQIA+ enlistees can be declared unfit for service under Article 18/b (personality disorders) and Article 17/b (reactive psychoses and neurotic disorders), and queer conscripts often conceal their orientation to avoid dedovshchina hazing.

Resident-facing support infrastructure includes the Gender Resource Center, a queer-feminist platform established in 2020 in response to the lack of safe space and resources for people of different genders and sexual orientations; Gender and Development, created in 2007, which runs local projects with the Ministry of Health; AZAD LGBT, which ran in-person programming in Baku including LGBTQ movie nights attended by a local psychologist who joined post-film Q&As and launched a website in 2015 with free online LGBTQ education tools; Minority Magazine's education coverage; and the Nafas LGBTI Azerbaijan Alliance, which regularly holds talks with the EU Delegation to Azerbaijan and other European embassies about the difficulties LGBTQ people face.

In April 2019 a 14-year-old girl from Baku attempted suicide after homophobic bullying at her school; the principal took no action, tried to attribute the attempt to family difficulties and did not call an ambulance, and she died in hospital two days later. The school director, deputy director and psychologist were dismissed, and on 24 October 2019 the Sabail District Court of Baku sentenced the principal to 2 years and 2.5 months of restricted liberty plus 18,500 AZN ($10,882) in compensation. The case prompted a nationwide social media campaign, a video by 2011 Eurovision winner Nigar Jamal addressed to President Ilham Aliyev, and a Ministry of Education anti-bullying action plan launched on 13 May 2019 with a new hotline to improve school-family relations and protect students from abuse.
outOfScopeNotes:
The constitution guarantees freedom of expression, and the Azerbaijan Press Council, founded in 2003, handles complaints under a Press Code of Conduct. It is not known whether the council has assessed complaints that state-controlled media used homosexuality to discredit government critics.

Whether men who have sex with men are de facto permitted to donate blood is not established by these sources; only the statutory exclusion of people infected with HIV/AIDS is documented.

No sourced material in this inventory addresses entry and visa procedures, document-marker checks at the border, or screening practice at Azerbaijani airports that treats trans or gender-nonconforming travellers differently. Nothing here should be read as describing that layer of contact.

The record documents individual incidents with dates but provides no trans-specific violence rate, no denominator and no comparison against the country's general homicide rate, so no magnitude of risk can be stated. The 2017 figures of at least 100 detained and at least 60 imprisoned or fined are raw counts from that single operation and are not a prevalence measure.
